title: Classifier-Free Guidance (CFG)
subtitle: Topic: Classifier-Free Guidance · Subject: Generative Modeling · Seven illustrated questions on conditional diffusion, conditioning dropout, the CFG formula, scale trade-offs, PyTorch inference, negative prompts, and evaluation.
hero:
CLASSIFIER-FREE GUIDANCE · GENERATIVE MODELING

Steer a diffusion model without training a separate classifier

Learn how prompt-conditioned and unconditioned predictions combine, why a guidance scale changes results, and how to measure quality without assuming stronger guidance is always better.

Conditional estimateUnconditional estimateGuided estimate

Conceptual diagram; prediction symbols refer to a noise-prediction model. Other prediction parameterizations and guidance formulations exist.

questions.stem: What is Classifier-Free Guidance (CFG) in diffusion-based Generative Modeling, and why can it steer generation without a separate image classifier?
options: Classifier-Free Guidance trains a separate classifier on noisy images, then uses its gradients to adjust the denoiser. It avoids text conditioning inside the generative network but still relies on classifier scores to direct each sampling step.

Classifier-Free Guidance adjusts sampling by repeating one conditional prediction at several noise levels. It avoids a separate classifier because the denoiser's own uncertainty score replaces the need for an unconditional prediction.

Classifier-Free Guidance combines a diffusion model's conditional and unconditional predictions to steer denoising toward a prompt. Both can come from one model trained with occasional dropped conditions, so no separate classifier is required.

Classifier-Free Guidance first denoises an image without text, then applies a learned caption classifier to select matching pixels. Classifier training is unnecessary because the text encoder evaluates only the final image after sampling.
questions.explanation: Explanation: Classifier-Free Guidance (CFG) steers diffusion sampling by combining predictions made with and without a condition, such as a text prompt. Unlike traditional classifier guidance, it needs no separately trained classifier whose gradient scores noisy images. A single denoiser can learn both branches by sometimes receiving a dropped condition during training. For example, an image model generating an owl on a mossy branch can strengthen the direction associated with that prompt while denoising. CFG changes inference predictions; it does not guarantee a perfect owl.
questions.figure:
01 · VISUAL LESSON

Two ways to guide diffusion: external classifier versus two denoiser predictions

Unlike classifier guidance, CFG does not require a separate noisy-image classifier. The same diffusion model can be evaluated with and without the condition, often in one batched inference call.

questions.stem: How does conditioning dropout during diffusion-model training enable both the conditional and unconditional predictions required by Classifier-Free Guidance?
options: During training, the model sometimes receives the real condition and sometimes a null condition, while learning the same denoising task. This teaches one set of weights to make conditional and unconditional predictions at inference time.

During training, the model drops all text for the first half of epochs and permanently restores it later. The early weights become a fixed unconditional network, and the later weights train a separate conditional network.

During training, the model replaces a random fraction of image pixels with blank pixels, teaching one denoiser to reconstruct missing content. At inference, those blank pixels act as the unconditional text embedding.

During training, dropout removes prompt words only from examples the model predicts incorrectly, so the denoiser learns a corrective negative prompt. The unconditional estimate is then calculated from the final image quality score.
questions.explanation: Explanation: Conditioning dropout means deliberately hiding the condition, such as a text embedding, for some training examples. The denoiser still predicts its noise target, learning how to work both with and without prompt information. At inference, it can produce two predictions for the same noisy latent and timestep. For example, a training set of ceramic-vase images might occasionally replace the vase description with a null condition. This teaches an unconditional baseline without a separately trained model. Drop probability is a training choice, not the guidance scale.
questions.figure:
02 · VISUAL LESSON

Training alternates labeled conditions and deliberately dropped conditions

Condition dropout teaches one network to predict with a prompt and with a null condition. It is stochastic during training; the drop probability is not the inference-time guidance scale.

questions.stem: How does the Diffusers-style Classifier-Free Guidance formula combine conditional and unconditional noise predictions, and what do guidance scales 1, 3, and 7 mean?
options: The formula subtracts the conditional prediction from the unconditional prediction and divides by guidance scale. At scale 1 the estimate is unconditional, while scales 3 and 7 progressively reduce attention to the requested prompt.

The formula averages conditional and unconditional estimates, then multiplies their sum by the guidance scale. Scale 1 yields the average prediction, while scales 3 and 7 mainly increase the amount of noise removed per step.

The formula adds the guidance scale to the conditional noise estimate and then subtracts unconditional variance. Scale 1 keeps the original prompt, while scales 3 and 7 add larger random perturbations instead of strengthening conditioning.

The formula is ε_guided = ε_uncond + s(ε_cond − ε_uncond). At s=1 it equals the conditional prediction; at s=3 or 7 it extrapolates farther in the conditioned direction, potentially increasing prompt influence.
questions.explanation: Explanation: A common Diffusers convention combines predictions using ε_guided = ε_uncond + s(ε_cond − ε_uncond). The two estimates must refer to the same noisy sample and timestep. When s=1 the result equals ε_cond; larger scales extrapolate in the conditional direction. For example, if a coral-reef model predicts 0.2 unconditionally and 0.5 conditionally for one noise component, s=1 gives 0.5, s=3 gives 1.1, and s=7 gives 2.3. These are numerical noise predictions, not image quality ratings.
questions.figure:
03 · VISUAL LESSON

The guidance formula moves past the conditional prediction

With ε_uncond=0.2 and ε_cond=0.5, the difference is 0.3. The formula gives 0.5 at s=1, 1.1 at s=3, and 2.3 at s=7. These are predicted noise values, not image-quality scores.

questions.stem: Why can increasing the CFG guidance scale improve prompt adherence but reduce diversity or create artifacts, and how should a useful scale be selected?
options: Increasing guidance makes conditional and unconditional predictions more similar, so high scales gradually remove text influence. A useful scale is chosen by maximizing diversity, because image quality remains stable as conditioning becomes weaker.

Increasing guidance strengthens the difference between conditional and unconditional predictions, often improving prompt alignment while reducing variety or amplifying artifacts. Compare several scales with matched prompts and seeds to choose a practical balance.

Increasing guidance improves adherence by adding more denoising steps and reducing the scheduler's learning rate. Strong guidance causes artifacts only when the image has too many objects, so selecting scale by object count is sufficient.

Increasing guidance directs each pixel toward the text embedding before the denoiser runs, eliminating uncertainty at high scales. Select the strongest supported scale because diversity and visual quality are unrelated to guidance magnitude.
questions.explanation: Explanation: Raising CFG scale extrapolates farther from an unconditional prediction toward the prompt-conditioned direction. This may make generated details fit the text better but can narrow variety or exaggerate textures, color, and contrast. The tradeoff depends on the model, scheduler, and prompt, so there is no universally best scale. For example, compare product illustrations of a sneaker at matched seeds and steps across several scales. Inspect whether the requested colors appear without distorted laces or excessive saturation. More guidance is not automatically better.
questions.figure:
04 · VISUAL LESSON

Low, moderate, and extreme guidance can trade freedom for artifacts

These are visual metaphors, not measured outputs. Guidance beyond the conditional branch can improve prompt fidelity, but increasing it indefinitely may increase oversaturation, distort detail, or reduce output diversity.

questions.stem: How can PyTorch implement CFG using paired denoiser predictions, and why must both predictions use the same noisy sample and diffusion timestep?
options: PyTorch implements CFG by multiplying the current latent tensor by guidance scale after a single conditional denoiser call. Keeping one timestep is sufficient, since unconditional estimates can be approximated from the latent magnitude afterward.

PyTorch implements CFG by subtracting the noise estimate from the final decoded image and scaling the resulting RGB pixels. The conditional and unconditional calls may use different timesteps because only their final pixel shapes must agree.

PyTorch can compute ε_uncond + s(ε_cond − ε_uncond) with matching noise-prediction tensors. Both estimates must use the same noisy latent and timestep so their difference reflects conditioning rather than changes in noise level or state.

PyTorch implements CFG by averaging predictions across different noisy latents and multiplying by the requested scale. Separate timesteps improve stability because the model sees more uncertainty before the conditional prediction is compared with the unconditional one.
questions.explanation: Explanation: CFG is implemented by taking conditional and unconditional denoiser outputs for the same noisy sample xₜ and timestep t, then combining them with a guidance scale. In PyTorch, ordinary tensor subtraction and multiplication implement the formula. Matching states is essential: otherwise the difference mixes prompt effects with unrelated changes in noise. For example, a synthetic three-component prediction yields [1.1, 1.1, −0.2] at scale 3 in the code below. This is a CPU-tested calculation, not a trained image generator.
questions.figure:
05 · VISUAL LESSON

Build the guided noise estimate from two PyTorch tensors

Python · guidance arithmetic 10 lines · CPU-tested · no model download
import torch
eps_uncond = torch.tensor([0.2, -0.1, 0.4])
eps_cond   = torch.tensor([0.5,  0.3, 0.2])
def guide(scale):
    return eps_uncond + scale * (eps_cond - eps_uncond)
for scale in (1.0, 3.0, 7.0):
    guided = guide(scale)
    print(scale, [round(v, 2) for v in guided.tolist()])
# Both predictions must use the same x_t and timestep.
# Example tensors only; no image model was run.
Verified first outputs: 1.0 → [0.5, 0.3, 0.2], 3.0 → [1.1, 1.1, -0.2], and 7.0 → [2.3, 2.7, -1.0]. This is an inference-combination example, not a trained generator.

Run this example to verify the precise CFG arithmetic. Real inference requires a trained denoiser to produce both predictions; multiplying latents or directly multiplying final RGB pixels is not CFG.

questions.stem: How do negative prompts, guidance rescaling, and guidance start–stop schedules modify CFG behavior, and why do they not guarantee unwanted content disappears?
options: Negative prompts can replace the baseline condition with an undesired concept; rescaling may reduce excessive prediction magnitudes, and schedules apply guidance during selected steps. These steer sampling but cannot guarantee that unwanted content vanishes.

Negative prompts remove prohibited image regions after diffusion has finished, while rescaling checks generated pixels against a classifier. Start–stop schedules alter video frame rate rather than the denoising process, so all three controls act independently of CFG.

Negative prompts train an extra classifier to reject unwanted features, while guidance rescaling lowers model temperature. Start–stop schedules increase the number of denoising steps, guaranteeing every excluded object is omitted when the scale is high enough.

Negative prompts subtract a fixed RGB pattern from the final picture; rescaling reduces image resolution to avoid overexposure. Guidance schedules apply only during training, making these controls irrelevant to the inference-time conditional and baseline predictions.
questions.explanation: Explanation: In supported CFG pipelines, a negative prompt can act as the baseline condition to steer generation away from specified concepts; it is not an absolute deletion rule. Guidance rescaling can moderate overexposure or excessive magnitudes at high scales. Start–stop schedules apply guidance during only part of denoising. For example, a poster prompt that discourages blurry lettering may still produce misspelled text. These controls change sampling tendencies; they do not replace checking the output. Availability and parameter behavior vary across pipelines.
questions.figure:
06 · VISUAL LESSON

Negative conditioning, rescaling, and guidance schedules solve different problems

Negative prompt ≠ deletion filterRescale ≠ smaller guidance scaleSchedules depend on pipeline

A negative prompt steers away from concepts but does not reliably prohibit them. Guidance rescaling can help extreme exposure; schedules may limit guidance to a fraction of denoising steps. These are implementation-dependent controls.

questions.tag: Advanced · Evaluation, efficiency, and safe use
questions.stem: How should CFG settings be evaluated for prompt adherence, diversity, image or video artifacts, inference cost, reproducibility, and responsible deployment?
options: CFG should be assessed mainly by a single text-image similarity metric, since high agreement proves that visual artifacts and diversity are acceptable. Inference cost is independent of unconditional predictions, and identical seeds always guarantee exact replication.

CFG should be selected from the sharpest single output at the largest available scale, then reused across languages, prompts, and videos. Reproducibility and safety follow naturally once the same text encoder and sampler are used.

CFG should be evaluated by how quickly images are produced, treating diversity as a side effect of training rather than sampling. Video results need only frame-level realism scores because temporal artifacts are determined by the video codec.

CFG should be compared across prompts and seeds for adherence, variety, artifacts, and reproducibility; video also needs temporal checks. Measure extra denoiser work and memory, and retain licensing, consent, safety reviews, and human oversight.
questions.explanation: Explanation: Evaluate CFG at several guidance scales using matched prompts, random seeds, samplers, and step counts. Check instruction-following, diversity, artifacts, latency, and memory, rather than relying on one pretty output. The two prediction branches can add compute, although batching and implementation choices matter. For a generated video showing a kite above a lake, inspect frame-to-frame identity and flicker as well as the prompt. Production also requires privacy, licensing, consent, and appropriate review of synthetic media. Repeatability may depend on hardware and library versions.
questions.figure:
07 · VISUAL LESSON

Judge guidance by prompt fidelity, diversity, artifacts, and compute

AdherenceObject attributes, layout, and prompt constraints
Fidelity & varietyArtifacts, diversity, saturation, subgroup failures
Cost & trustLatency, memory, consent, licensing, misuse

CFG often requires conditional and unconditional denoiser predictions, increasing computation compared with one branch. Benchmark prompt-specific outcomes, not just one attractive image; video tasks also need temporal-consistency checks.
